opening.speaker: neet

options.teaser: The fever cart is coughing at the gate, and the red shelf has been leaned on hard this week.
Two of the blue-herb beds carry labels nobody can read anymore.
A heavy yellow-herb season is coming, and the drying loft groans when the wind does.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: Neet takes the assignment and goes; whatever happens out there comes home with her.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: The trip is over. Open Neet's report to see what happened, and how it ended.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The fever cart coughs at the gate, and the shrine's red shelf has been leaned on hard this week. Neet walks the whole shelf before promising anyone anything.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Red herbs, then. The whole road is coughing, and this week has leaned hard on the red shelf. I will promise nothing until the shelf and the road have both had their say.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts past the gate, where the fever cart rolled just ahead, its driver shaking his head over a wrapper-stripped shelf.

returnBeats.speaker: driver
returnBeats.text: Whole road's coughing. Two stops behind yours.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: He has nothing to sell her. The strong batch's last measured share rides in her basket, weighed out on the shelf walk this morning.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Next on his round, the settlement: its strong beds stripped bare weeks ago - every root that promised speed bought the minute the coughing began.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: What remains is the settlement's own kitchen-row patch of mild red leaf, planted for household coughs: same root, slower in the cup, unwanted all season because the fever has everyone buying fast.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: A grandmother has held the queue since dawn, three grandchildren coughing in turns.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Neet counts her basket against it and sees the arithmetic nobody says aloud: not enough.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: One bargain, plainly, then: the strong share in my basket, weighed to two jars, for the whole spare cutting of the mild row.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The grandmother looks at the strong bundle, then at Neet.

returnBeats.speaker: grandmother
returnBeats.text: It's the same root, girl. Just slower.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: And the fever does not wait.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: They shake hands on it - two jars for the row - and Neet pays the two, adding nothing beyond the price they named.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: By her count on the walk home, the mild cutting is four times the leaf she left with: slower by half, but the same root.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She reorders the red shelf by urgency instead of alphabet - fever jars nearest the door - and quietly refills the first kit before anyone asks. 'Urgent first' becomes the shelf rule, and the first kit has never been short since.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: Two of the blue-herb beds carry labels nobody can read anymore. Neet agrees to straighten the beds without agreeing to trust them.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Blue herbs, then. Two beds, two unreadable labels, and no reason yet to trust either. I will straighten what is crooked and promise to trust nothing.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the beds: the real trouble is the ledger, and it kept the bad ink's story, reading the sunward bed as mild and the shaded bed as strong.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Dosed by the ledger's story, the strong crop plays mild and the mild plays strong - half a remedy or a double one - and the seed saved from its 'best' bed would plant the error again.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Neet tastes a leaf from each - one bitter first, then cold, the other answering differently - but the hot dry week slurs the harvests; a tongue can say the crops differ, not whose story is true.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The two wait in separate cups. Mena, the youngest volunteer, finally comes off the wall.

returnBeats.speaker: mena
returnBeats.text: I watered both beds the year before the labels went. The mean, bitter leaf always came off the sunward bed - the one the ledger reads as mild.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Scolded, she says, for overwatering the shaded one - and she kept the two straight ever since. She gives it up like a small crime confessed.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: I will not taste again - the tongue said its all. Your account is testable another way: an overwatered bed keeps its drenching.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: So Neet walks where Mena says she stood with the can - and then walks the rest. The short haul from the water barrel to the shaded bed is worn bare by a year of full cans, the ground there still draining late.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The sunward bed has no such road - no worn haul, no water path, no late drain. Ground sides with memory: shaded bed pampered, sunward bed mean and bitter - the ledger backward all along.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: So the sun remembers even when the ink did not. Then we will not correct you. We will write you down.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She re-inks every label, then does the unfashionable thing: corrects the bed-ledger to match the truth of the beds, not the habit of the ledger. The bed-ledger tells the truth again, and the label ink she mixed is the one still in use.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: A heavy yellow-herb season is coming, and the drying loft groans when the wind does. Neet inspects the loft before the first load goes up.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Yellow herbs, then. A heavy season is coming, and the loft already complains about the wind. I will walk it before the first load goes up.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the loading yard, where the first yellow-herb load comes off the cart wrong: this year's cut is sap-heavy, taken young and wet because the fields came late and the shrine ordered early.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The same trays that went up light as chaff last year now take both hands, and Neet weighs one against her hip before she says anything at all.

returnBeats.speaker: grower
returnBeats.text: They will dry lighter than they travel.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Which is exactly the trouble - the loft has to carry them at their heaviest.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Before the first load went up, she walked the empty loft end to end and found nothing the eye could fault - the wind's groan unexplained.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: Level, unloaded, and quiet about it. I will walk it again when it is carrying.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Inside, volunteers are loading at a speed that means nobody has counted the load.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Neet watches one tray go up and hears the beam take it with a sound she does not like - a long wooden note, the kind furniture makes before it stops being furniture.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She stops the next tray at the bottom of the stair.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: We will count what goes up, before the loft decides we did not.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The volunteers look caught rather than annoyed. Gorram, the oldest, has hauled yellow bundles all morning and does not stop to argue.

returnBeats.speaker: gorram
returnBeats.text: Nothing ever fell in thirty years.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Which is what everyone always says about beams. Neet climbs anyway, walks the loft heel to heel with a measuring string, and finds the middle beam carrying more than its share, a thumb's width below its brothers.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She marks it in chalk, sorts the wettest yellow bundles onto the side beams, and puts the string back where the next hand will find it and wonder.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She doubles the braces, ropes the racks, and - because a loft that holds more invites people - leaves a bench in the warm corner. The loft holds double, and rain-guests still sleep there by custom.

opening.text: Before the dew lifts, then. I have the knives, the baskets, and a ledger with empty pages. Tell me what we gather, and I will be ready.

options.teaser: Dense caps the soup pot has been asking for - the kind that survive a tumble in the basket.
The beds have been acting suspicious all week, and the mushrooms present themselves far too neatly.
Springy beneath their spotted caps, and already climbing out of the crates this morning.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: Neet takes the assignment and goes; whatever happens out there comes home with her.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: The trip is over. Open Neet's report to see what happened, and how it ended.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The shrine soup pot wants sturdy caps, and the porter's basket always seems lighter on the way back up. Neet decides to weigh the basket once, out of politeness.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Sturdy caps, then. The pot feeds the pilgrims, and I would rather check a scale than guess at supper. We leave before the dew lifts.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The ravine gave its usual account: dense caps off the fallen oaks, wide clusters culled, half of every log left standing. One dropped cap took its gravel tumble on the way home and was no worse than a scuff.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: At the gate Harl the porter comes up the switchback, one basket, the pickers' tally slip riding the rim. She asks to carry it the last few yards, out of politeness, and the weight reads wrong in her grip.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She weighs it once at the kitchen scale, thanking him for the loan, then sets today's beside the delivery weights her ledger has kept for weeks.

returnBeats.speaker: harl
returnBeats.text: Full at the ravine, lighter by the gate. I have been telling my arms they are getting old.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The ledger has agreed with you for weeks. A shortfall that keeps its size could come from habit, cargo, or the basket itself, and nothing yet tells me which. I would like to weigh your basket again - may I?

returnBeats.speaker: harl
returnBeats.text: Weigh it, then. It came up the same switchback as always.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The apology is drafted for the asking, not for any finding: questioning a guest's basket costs something, and she will pay it.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The page takes two columns - what the tally slips promise, what the scale confirms. This side stays blank for morning.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Harl leaves the basket beside the kitchen scale for the night.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: A false bottom has been shorting the count for weeks; she double-counts by weight, catches it kindly, and cooks nothing until every cap is accounted. Jars of sturdy-cap soup go out to the pilgrims, and the twice-counted rule becomes the children's first lesson in counting anything.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The clever mushrooms present themselves for labeling, which is exactly how Neet knows they are lying. The beds have been acting suspicious all week.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Clever mushrooms, then. If they mean to be counted, they can be counted properly. I will bring stakes and a straight hand.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The beds have been presenting themselves all week: caps curled generously outward, white stems standing to be counted, everything turned toward the path by hands nobody can name.

returnBeats.speaker: sedge
returnBeats.text: I have watched them all week. Too neat to trust.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The obvious, orderly thing first, then: stakes and a straight line of soil.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The first never touches soil: the nearest cap folds into the leaf litter flat and final, between one blink and the next, without a sound. She tries the second bed and gets the same shallow theater.

returnBeats.speaker: sedge
returnBeats.text: They only do it when the stakes come out. It is not the watching they mind. I stood over them all Tuesday.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: So she rolls the label into its leather and stands at the path with her hands folded, and the beds remember themselves - up, curled, guilty.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: A label nobody will hold still for keeps nothing. A mushroom that lies about itself still tells the truth about where it will not stand.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The week's refusals are the better record: the patch by the warm stone keeps its distance, and the patch under the drip-line grows nowhere wet.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She maps the refusals in the day's margin and pencils one line of a rhyme beside them, to hear whether rhythm can keep what stakes cannot: it will not stand where the drip-line lands. The third stake stays in the drawer, on purpose.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: They keep flattening into leaf litter at the first touch of a label, so she stops labeling and starts rhyming, sorting by where they refuse to grow. A basket is collected in order, and the sorting rhyme enters the children's lesson, where it is credited to the mushrooms.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The lively mushrooms have been escaping crates since dawn, and the downhill trip to the village is today. Neet checks the rope twice.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Lively mushrooms, then. The pantry's pickling day does not move for anyone, and the crates have been making their own arrangements since dawn. I will check the rope twice.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the loading, before the cart left. The cooper stood there with four lids he had already named a favor.

returnBeats.speaker: cooper
returnBeats.text: Nothing gets out of my crates.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: Which is true and not the point: a lid settles every argument in the dark, and a shortfall keeps its own counsel until the far end. If one gets out today, it gets out in daylight, where the getting-out has witnesses.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She hands the lids back.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: So the crates ride out open, under rope - spans anchored to the cooper's hoop-nails, woven wide enough to see through.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She checks it once at the gate and once at the hairpin, half for the knots, half for the mushrooms, who are owed a fair fence.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: On the bend one cap takes the bounce as a dare, clears the first span, and is caught by the second.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Past the village's first roofs the crates keep their drumroll, ropes humming at every spring. At the pantry step she sets them down still arguing, and the lids stay home in the shed. She does not trust what she cannot watch.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She lattices the crates with rope - not lids: rope, so the jumping is visible and the failure honest. Not one loss goes on the record, and the village pantry copies her lattice by month's end.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: The orchard has harvest rows to pick, and this morning the helping is Neet's.

opening.speaker: neet
opening.text: Before the dew lifts, then. I have the ledger, the sacks, and the day for it. Tell me where the orchard wants me, and I will be ready.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: Choose what Neet helps with today.

options.teaser: Bright fruit that pays its pickers in bruises, and a hired crew that will not admit their arms ache.
Three scales that have been disagreeing since harvest began, and three pickers each certain of a different one.
A fragrant fruit hanging farthest out, on ladders old enough to wobble worst beneath it.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: Neet takes the assignment and goes; whatever happens out there comes home with her.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: The trip is over. Open Neet's report to see what happened, and how it ended.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The power rows pay pickers in bruises, and the hired crew will not admit their arms ache. Neet is working the row and watching arms instead of fruit.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Fruit of power, then. I will work the row I am given and watch the arms around me. The fruit lends its strength; the pickers should keep some of their own.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the power rows, where the hired crew has been at it since before light: bright fruit, heavy sacks, and a pace that does not slacken because nobody has told it to.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Neet takes the row she is given and picks with them, watching arms: shoulders rolled mid-lift, one picker carrying with the left arm only, a wrist flexed behind a sack while Tansy, the crew's fastest, is looking elsewhere.

returnBeats.speaker: tansy
returnBeats.text: Nobody here is sore, cleric. Arms that complain do not get rehired, and we intend to be here next autumn.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: Then the orchard is luckier than most. The arms I watched rolled their shoulders eleven times between one tree and the next - I counted, because counting is what I was doing instead of complaining.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The crew's arithmetic runs on the rehiring: a sore arm is a short sack, a short sack is a season's end, so the aching gets folded away and picked through.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: My arms are new to this row and would like a minute at the row's end. Any arm wanting the same minute is welcome to share it. The sacks will wait - they always do.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The minute starts as hers alone. Then another picker sets down his sack, then two more, and Tansy stands holding her own wrist at the row's end, not admitting to anything and resting all the same.

returnBeats.speaker: tansy
returnBeats.text: One minute, then. But the sacks will hear none of it from me.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Neet keeps her ledger open against a sack through the afternoon: which arms gave out first, and which minute brought them back.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She sets a rest rota nobody asked for and stocks a cold-compress barrel at the row's end. The rows finish before dark, and the rota quietly becomes the orchard's autumn custom - signed, as everything of hers is, with a small tidy hand.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The wisdom grove's scales have been disagreeing since harvest began, and three pickers are arguing over which one to believe. Neet brings a notebook instead of an opinion.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Fruit of wisdom, then. Three scales arguing is three chances to count well. I will bring the notebook and ask each scale the same question - more than once, if they mean it.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the wisdom grove: three scales within shouting distance, and three pickers camped one to a scale, each sure the other two are being robbed.

returnBeats.speaker: pell
returnBeats.text: The gate scale is honest. It weighed my mule true for the farrier, and it has weighed my sacks since the rows were young.

returnBeats.speaker: wray
returnBeats.text: The grove scale is honest. The gate one reads proud - it has been saying half again what my sacks carry since harvest began.

returnBeats.speaker: thirdpicker
returnBeats.text: The yard scale has outlived four owners. It is the honest one.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: Then we will ask each scale the same question more than once, and then ask it again with a different load. A notebook weighs nothing, and it does not take sides.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The same fruit from her basket crosses to all three scales and back, three rounds each, while the pickers watch like judges. Every scale repeats itself to the ounce - and repeats its disagreement, the same way every round.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Then a different load crosses the same three scales - a sack of Pell's, surrendered growling - and the three answers come back in the same pattern again. Whatever the scales are doing, they do it steadily.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: None of them is random, so none of them has to lose. A scale that answers steadily can be corrected for - keep your scales, and we will write down each one's manner until the numbers can be trusted across the grove.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: So the notebook takes a page of manners, one line per scale, and the argument becomes arithmetic instead of war. Pell keeps his gate scale, Wray keeps his grudge with a number attached, and the pickers go back to their ladders.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: From then on, every reading that reaches her book can be made to speak with the others, and the pickers start bringing their numbers to be read unasked. The notebook went home heavier than it came.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She records pick-weight by row and hour, and finds the east rows sweeten early in shade. The picking order is rebuilt around her notes - the ledger doing the diplomacy she never learned.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The spirit fruit hangs farthest out, and the old ladders beneath it wobble worst. Neet looks at the ladder feet first and the fruit second.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Fruit of spirit, then. The fruit can hang; the ladders cannot wait. I will look at the feet first and let the fruit take its turn.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the far rows: the spirit trees are the oldest in the orchard, the fruit hangs farthest out, and the ladders leaning under them are older than the pickers.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She looks at the feet first, as she said she would: half the feet are worn round, one leg stands shorter where rot has been at work, and the grass beneath is stamped with years of the same small sway.

returnBeats.speaker: tam
returnBeats.text: The fruit is not coming down to meet us, cleric. Are we picking, or are we carpentering?

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: Both, while the ladders keep their opinions. A wobble at the feet is a picker on the ground by noon. Hold the fruit in your head; I will have this one honest in a minute.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The first ladder gets the full attention: wedges under the worn feet, a rope collar at the top rung, and her whole weight testing each leg before it earns her basket.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She climbs it herself with the first basket, and the ladder takes her weight without comment. Tam watches the rungs the whole way up and forgets to be unimpressed.

returnBeats.speaker: tam
returnBeats.text: All right. Do mine next - the tall one by the wall has danced with me twice this week.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The crew groans at the speed of it, and the grumbling keeps time with the work all afternoon. The far fruit comes down fragrant and unhurried.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The last baskets come down at the pace the ladders allow, and Tam loses a race to one of them, which the crew rules the correct order of things.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She braces every leg and ropes every top rung, no shortcuts taken even while the crew groans at the pace. Nobody falls; the brace pattern is saved under the barn for next season.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: The winds have been generous all week, and the feather work is Neet's.

opening.speaker: neet
opening.text: Before the dew lifts, then. I have the basket, the ledger, and a morning that wants walking. Tell me where the wind is leaving things, and I will be ready.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: Choose what Neet gathers today.

options.teaser: Bright feathers drifting along the mill path like scattered festival litter - and Neet walking it with a basket and a plan.
Bluebird feathers are being graded wet and sold dry, and the arguments about color have outlasted the colors.
Where the heath path climbs, the winter wind has been dropping old wyvern feathers for weeks - and Neet wants them gathered honestly.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: Neet takes the assignment and goes; whatever happens out there comes home with her.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: The trip is over. Open Neet's report to see what happened, and how it ended.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: Rainbow bird feathers have been drifting along the mill path all week, bright as scattered festival litter. Neet is walking it with a basket and a plan.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Rainbow feathers, then. Bright things the wind is handing out for free, and a basket to receive them properly. I will walk the path slowly enough to notice.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts on the mill path, where the wind has been scattering for days: rainbow feathers lying bright across the ruts, trodden at the wheel's edge, and still coming down.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She walks it as slow as its bends want, picking up what the ruts have not ruined, and listening: pilgrims pass both ways, and more than one of them stoops.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: An old pilgrim with a stick, Maren, stops mid-climb to lift one feather out of a puddle and press it flat between her palms, drying something worth drying.

returnBeats.speaker: maren
returnBeats.text: One each, that is the custom of the path. Take two and your neighbor's luck goes short. Mine has ridden in my book since the winter of the feast and it still works.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The arithmetic of the path is in its ditches: luck goes to whoever stoops first, and the brightest feathers rot in the hedges where nobody will reach.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Nearer the top, a young pilgrim named Ansel straggles up against the cold, thin bundle on his back, hands red at the knuckles.

returnBeats.speaker: ansel
returnBeats.text: I have come up twice and gone down twice, and the wind has not let me keep one yet. My hands have not let go of the cold either.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: That is luck going into ditches and cold sleeves. A feather carried alone warms one walk and fades. Sewn down among many, it would warm every walk after - and I mean to start the circle that does that sewing.

returnBeats.speaker: maren
returnBeats.text: Then the custom sleeps easy. It rations the feathers a person carries for luck, and yours are going into common work, not into any pocket - nobody's luck goes short while your basket fills. Take the muddy ones too; mud cleans off.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The walk back down takes longer than the walk up: the wind is generous, the mud is persuasive, and her basket rides heavier every field.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She gathers the feathers for a pilgrims' quilting circle of her own starting, washing and sorting by warmth rather than shade. The circle is founded on one basket of fetched luck - the first of the region's comfort-works, as she writes in the margin - and it is still the warmest.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: Bluebird feathers are being graded wet and sold dry, and the market's arguments about color have outlasted the colors. Neet is asked to look at the evidence.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Bluebird feathers, then. Colors that change with their weather need comparing, not arguing. One feather, graded wet, dried, and graded once more - same eyes, and the page will keep both answers.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the market, where a crate of bluebird feathers has been bought, returned, disputed, and resold until the argument is older than the feathers in it.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The stallkeepers sent for her the way a street sends for its cleric: Vetch, senior among the graders, walks her to the crate himself and lays the whole grievance flat.

returnBeats.speaker: vetch
returnBeats.text: Grade it wet, sell it dry, and every side remembers a different bird. I have argued color until color is all we argue about. You were sent for. Show me what the feathers have been doing while we were talking.

returnBeats.speaker: dov
returnBeats.text: A feather is bluest when it comes off the bird, and that is what I grade. If the blue fades on somebody's windowsill, that is drying, not cheating.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: Then we will stop arguing about honesty and start arguing about states. One feather, graded wet and graded dry by Dov's own eyes, with the drying in between. If a grade moves with its drying, that much at least is settled.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Dov grades the first feather wet, and it reads blue as a patch of clear sky, as his way goes. Neet writes the grade on her page with the word wet beside it.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The feather dries on the stall's warm slate while the market holds its breath. Read again by Dov, same eyes, same light, it comes back a shade short of clear sky, and the two grades share a line on her page.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: A second feather goes through the same round - wet, dried, read again - and lands a shade short by the same amount. Dov looks at his own hands as if they had been keeping secrets from him.

returnBeats.speaker: vetch
returnBeats.text: A shade short, twice, by the same amount. So there is weather in the argument - a source we can write down, where before we only traded memories.

returnBeats.speaker: dov
returnBeats.text: Grade them wet if it suits you, sell them dry if it suits the day, but write which state a grade is in - and I will put my name to mine.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Neet closes her ledger on the morning: two feathers, four grades, one drying slate, and not one word of argument spent on honesty.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She catalogs wet-light against dry-light and writes the difference into her ledger. Every later dispute ends before it starts; the market graders ask for a copy, and it sits beside hers.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: Where the heath path climbs, the winter wind has been shedding old wyvern feathers for weeks. Neet wants them for the shrine stores, and wants them gathered honestly.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Wyvern feathers, then. I want them honestly come by - what the wind finished with, and nothing newer. A heath like that deserves a local arm beside me, and I will ask for one.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts where the heath path climbs: the winter wind has been laying old feathers along it for weeks, and the gatherers read the drifts the way farmers read weather.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The gatherers lend her Sarn, a heath gatherer with a hooked stick and no hurry, and the climb begins at the pace the path allows.

returnBeats.speaker: sarn
returnBeats.text: Three rules on the heath. Walk where the stones can be seen, take what the wind has finished with, and never argue with a wyvern's weather.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Old-shed shows itself at the quill: papery at the root, light as a year of weather. At the first patch of fresh shed she pauses, then leaves it where it fell - the wyvern is not finished with it, and neither is she.

returnBeats.speaker: sarn
returnBeats.text: There is a door in the heath, as we say. The goat track. It drops two bends of path, and every winter it drops somebody with them. The wind stacks feathers on it too - pretty ones, fresh ones.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: Then the door stays shut. We are not late enough to trade a winter's caution for forty minutes, and the fresh ones are not ours. The kept path ends where the job ends - I will walk it whole.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The kept path goes the long way and the long way pays: old feathers lie thick along the stones, and once the light opens far above and something long and golden crosses it, and the heath stands still until it is past.

returnBeats.speaker: sarn
returnBeats.text: That is why the heath has gatherers and not heroes. You walked it properly today, cleric. The feathers under your arm are all the storm's old furniture, and the path will remember you walking it.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: By the wall at the bottom she makes the morning into a page in her ledger: rules kept, fresh refused, one wing overhead, and a weight of old-shed that will need sorting before it is anything at all.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She walks the marked path with an escort and refuses every shortcut, taking old-shed only. The winter stores gain a wyvern line, and the heath path earns its first marker stone.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: The frost came early and did not send word ahead. By the first hard night, three wild clutches - bright as a rumor, singing in the dark, far too large for anyone's comfort - had come down from the high nests.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: They came down onto the one crag by the orchard, on a shelf of stone already leaning toward winter. Nobody owns wild things - that is the law of the region, and also the excuse of anyone who owes a favor.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: By the hour before dawn, five keepers held the same freezing watch - a shrine keeper, a warrior, a knight, a baker, a challenger - giant opinions, empty hands. The ledge would not wait, and neither, in the end, did anyone.

opening.speaker: neet
opening.text: So the ledger opens on a cold page, and the writing is mine to keep - three clutches, one frost, no owner anywhere in it. Tell me which egg I am minding until daylight, and I will write the night honestly.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: Choose the egg Neet's night will follow.
opening.note: Only options whose egg family is unlocked at this tier are shown; one, two, or three options are all valid states. This is one shared event, The Cold Roost: the opening lines are true whichever egg is chosen, and each chosen telling covers what the week did for all three clutches. No route is canon-locked; the other eggs stay available on later trips. The chosen egg is the story's focus, never a settlement award.

options.teaser: Bright as a rumor, and loosest of the three on a shelf the frost is already testing.
Singing to itself in the dark - the smallest voice on the crag tonight.
Far too large for anyone's comfort, and the ledge under it is losing its grip on winter.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: Neet takes the assignment and goes; whatever happens out there comes home with her.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: The trip is over. Open Neet's report to see what happened, and how it ended.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The rainbow clutch's crisis was never cold alone - it was custody. Wild things do not accept strange eggs on the strength of a speech about community.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: Custody first, then. Warmth will have its own hands on this crag; the introductions are mine to make. You cannot hurry a crag into liking somebody - you can only arrange the meeting, and I intend to pay the mornings it asks for.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the crag. The frost knocked the rainbow clutch free of its high nest before anyone had noticed it sat light there; by morning, the strange eggs lay cooling among ordinary ones, bright as sugar.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She walked the ledges with her ledger and counted the neighbors. Every nest up there belonged to somebody, and no argument she could write would move an egg.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The introductions will be made, not argued: a feather from the rainbow nest carried nose to nose, morning by morning, until the crag's birds read strangers as tenants. Nobody consents to a speech; everybody consents to a smell they know.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Daisy took the cold half of the problem: the ledge bricked in oven-warmed straw, heat only, tested against her cheek like checking proof, and every strange egg turned a quarter-twist twice a day, the way she steadies dough through its rise.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The first straw blanket went out too thick and insulated worse, and Daisy's answer to it became a sentence the ledger keeps in full.

returnBeats.speaker: daisy
returnBeats.text: That is all right. We can try again another time.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The first evening's work was testing how much weight the crag's stone would hold: Dolbur hauled himself up a rope and dropped the coil back down, and Kyle caught it one-handed.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: An introduction, Dolbur called it; a catch, said Kyle, more precisely - and they have opened with it ever since.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The high nest has been empty long enough; the mother is not coming back. I wrote it in my margin, not aloud, and kept one rainbow feather for the fledging day.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: By the third morning, the crag had stopped noticing which eggs were strange: the introductions held, nose to feathered nose, and the ledges rode warm.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The rainbow chicks hatched into borrowed warmth, the bluebird and wyvern eggs hatched without incident the same week, and every egg of the frost came out of its shell safe.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: When the fledging came, the rainbow chicks spread over the whole roost - among bluebirds and along the wyvern family's edges - until the roost considered itself mixed, and did not stop to think when it had started.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The roost's hatch-day goes into the shrine almanac tonight, in my own hand - the same hand as the margin note and the kept feather - and red, blue, and gold tellings begin their three-version record beside it.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Before the company scattered, Claire named the crag and reclassified it protected - the patrol schedule went up on the spot, in her handwriting, which is how the site held onto everything that happened there.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The frost, by Claire's log, broke inside the week and left the orchard untouched - trellis, fence, and fruit without a lasting scar.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: And the roost's lasting answer to the frost is beauty: every spring the fledglings' rainbow feathers turn up catching light along the orchard trellis, and the town walks out to see them - a mixed roost made famous, mostly, by its colors.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The bluebird clutch dulled overnight - shells gone from paint-bright to wet chalk, the song inside failing. Not an enemy, not a tangle, not a wind: a song losing its note.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: A song losing its note is no puzzle for paper. I will begin with the correct lullabies, as the rite teaches - and if the nest refuses the neatness, I will try the note it asks for instead.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the crag before dawn: the bluebird clutch dulled overnight, the other two merely cooling, and on the far ledge a wyvern egg working loose - one event, three needs.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Every need had its keeper inside the week. Dolbur offered loudly to fight the frost; he was politely assigned elsewhere.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Neet led with the shrine's lullabies, every line of them correct - and the nest flatly refused each one; the chick sat through three correct verses and went duller with each.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: So the rite would be a heresy, and the first one I ever intend to keep. Not flat as a mistake - flat where the song rises, on purpose, until the note inside matches me instead of me matching it.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The wrong note needed practice. At midnight, in the shrine pantry, where her voice carries least, she worked the flat note until it sat where she wanted it.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: For the record: my midnight voice carries a little further than the pantry believes. The bakery was kind about it, and I am polite about not knowing they heard.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Then the rite ran, wrong by design: flat where the song rises, until the note inside matched her error and held it. Within two nights the shells brightened out of their wet chalk.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The rest was quiet logistics. Kyle wound cloth around the ladder's metal rungs so nothing would ring, and then held a still vigil for hours at a stretch while the rite ran.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: She counted the only way her ear can - by what interrupted: over the two nights of wrong verses, nothing rose from the wrapped rungs to answer, and the hush around her note did not shift once.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Daisy restocked the leaning ledges with oven-warmed straw, heat only, so the other two clutches rode warm; the bakers' quarter stayed muffled, and warm bread came down so nobody had to shout a meal.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Claire kept three nights of silence and wrote the rule the moment asked for: no voices past the tree line.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: On the coldest night, Kyle's ladder-foot slid on the icy rock; Dolbur, out on the high path taking the frost-line reading, dropped his spare rope down, and Kyle caught it mid-slip. Both called it an introduction; neither called it a rescue.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The almanac gets the hatch-day. The rite record gets the method, exactly as run. What neither record gets is the margin note: some things mend when you stop correcting them.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: By the week's end every egg of the frost had hatched safe, and the roost's hatch-days went into the shrine almanac - red, blue, and gold - in the same tidy hand.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The frost broke inside the week and left the orchard without lasting damage. When the quiet held, the crag - named, protected - went onto the patrol schedule in Claire's hand: the site that asked for hush would get a watch.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The chick hatched healthy and sang flat all spring - the crag's mornings led by one patient bluebird - and its true song came back only after winter, the season the region remembers as quiet.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: What stayed was this: the wrong-lullaby rite on the shrine's records as a working rite, and a town that walks the orchard path hushed at nesting time, every spring.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The wyvern egg has rolled loose along the failing ledge's lip, and the other two clutches shiver through the frost. The mother came down circling - wide, patient, in no mood for committee.

departureBeats.speaker: neet
departureBeats.text: No climb moves one stone without her leave. I will have the compresses ready, a settling word learned by midnight, and her own signs read before anything shifts.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the crag, with a rule of the place: nothing up there moves without the mother's leave, and the night's first work is learning what her leave looks like.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The mother's circling invited no advice: Claire's cordons closed the orchard path and every roofline a spectator might use, and the region's people, to their credit, stayed behind them.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Dolbur climbed the winter-hardened rock, and one piton bent on the first reach. He reported it before his boots were down, immediately and cheerfully - which is half of why the climb worked.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: He had started early because he had heard her first - a sound like stone getting annoyed, he said - so the climb was half-rigged while everyone else was still deciding who would climb.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Kyle anchored from the storeroom's spare rope and counted every carry. Neet's part was quieter: compresses and a settling word readied long before they were needed, and her eyes on the mother's wings and tail for the right hour.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The lesson I learned and kept to myself: approach when her wings folded, wait when her tail set. One wrong guess and the committee convenes itself - and the ledger can suffer a blank when patience is the entry.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The hour was not ours to decide. Daisy had been up all night regardless, and what she carried out at first light settled the argument better than words could: a loaf, set down on the warm stone at the quarry's foot.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The mother circled once more over the stone, landed beside the loaf, and the landing decided it: the move went ahead under her leave.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Four carries later - dry stone, no blasting in its history, room to turn around - the brood was whole at the old quarry ledge, and the mother's next circle was drawn around them.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The carry baskets were lined with oven-warmed straw, heat only - the roost trick, by week's end, had earned its second career as courier-bedding.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: My margin, kept for myself: she was never guarding the old ledge. She was deciding whether the quarry was good enough - and the quarry was. Four carries say so better than I did.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: When the gear came down, the last coil dropped from the ledge straight into Kyle's waiting hands.

returnBeats.speaker: neet
returnBeats.text: The landing finished the argument, so I sent the only sign-off I had: one nod, from the correct distance, at a wyvern's eye level. It is not in any record, hers or ours.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The roost's hatch-days went into the shrine almanac as they came, one line beside the red and blue entries, in the same tidy hand as the rest of the frost week's bookkeeping.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: When Claire's cordons came down, they came down into something: the crag - named, protected - went onto the patrol schedule in her handwriting, and the quarry ledge went onto the map.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The frost broke inside seven days and left the orchard untouched. The moved egg hatched safe at the quarry - the first brood its new household ever raised - and the other two clutches hatched untroubled on the crag.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The crag lost a tenant and gained a neighbor: the wyvern household lives at the quarry ledge now, a fixed point on the map, on an adjusted patrol route - and the one the mother tolerates is Dolbur.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: And the first sentence of every version of that week stays the same, in the almanac and everywhere it is copied: nobody owns wild things.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: The trailside herb jobs are waiting this morning, and the herb work is Dolbur's.

opening.speaker: dolbur
opening.text: Trail day! Boots, pack frame, and rope, all checked by hand this morning. Point me at the herb, and I will make the trip worth talking about.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: Choose which herb sends Dolbur out.

options.teaser: The clinic's red order is urgent, and Dolbur's known shortcut is technically a trail.
Birds are working the blue patch from the air, and the assigned defense is one loud voice.
The yellow bundles are heavier than they look, and a single-trip record has already been announced.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: Dolbur takes the assignment and goes; whatever happens out there comes home with him.

dispatch.speaker: narrator
dispatch.text: The trip is over. Open Dolbur's report to see what happened, and how it ended.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The trail clinic wants red herbs, and Dolbur knows a shortcut that is technically a trail. He is halfway down it already.

departureBeats.speaker: dolbur
departureBeats.text: Red herbs, then! The shortcut is the shorter line, and I have run it plenty of times without complaint. The clinic will have its red well before the kettle sings.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the fork, reached twice: Dolbur had dropped halfway down the shortcut alone, then climbed back when a hiker - out for the day and glad of company that knows the hill - turned up at the sign.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Confident from the test run, he offered the faster line - his boots had just proved it - and the hiker took it, pace set by the boots ahead.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The far ledge was the shortcut's honest half: shelf rock with nobody's care on it, a crossing only his boots had ever learned. The step there that held his weight all season went loose under an ankle it had never met.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The hiker went down hard on the shelf, hands first, ankle swelling in the time a step takes twice. The line had made his offer sound safe; now it had to own the difference.

returnBeats.speaker: dolbur
returnBeats.text: The report comes first, and it is mine: my shortcut, my line, and a crossing stone nobody tends. The ankle turned on all three. I am sorry. Hold still - the carry is mine, and the splint waits at the clinic.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Then he went back over the same crossing with a passenger: the hiker up on his back, every step on the line his own boots knew, and the apology running under it the whole way - low, steady, and pointed at himself.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: At the clinic, the splint came third: board, wrap, and strap set by his own hands at the senior's word. Then the desk got the same report he gave on the ledge - shortcut named, crossing named, fault taken twice.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The evening went into his kit: splint board first, then wraps, tape, a spare cord, and the list pinned where his hands could find it without asking his memory. That afternoon the only splint board in reach had belonged to the clinic.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: A hiker's ankle turns on the far ledge, and the shortcut is the reason. He reports the wrong turn first, carries them back second, splint third, apology throughout. Every hunt after starts with a splint kit check, which the town clinic calls his finest invention and he calls overdue paperwork.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The blue-herb patch by the trail head is being raided bird by bird, and Dolbur has been assigned six rows to defend with his voice.

departureBeats.speaker: dolbur
departureBeats.text: Blue herbs, then! Six rows, one voice, and an assignment I cannot refuse: I am the defense. The birds are about to get the loudest afternoon the patch has ever heard.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts on the watch: he opened the defense at a volume that carries across three fields, calling the six rows to order one by one and declaring every leaf's interest to the whole valley.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The birds came anyway, and they came on a timetable: every raid ran in the pause after a bellow. By the third pass it was plain - the noise had edges, and the raid lived in them.

returnBeats.speaker: dolbur
returnBeats.text: Ha - my own timetable, reading me back! Fine: the volume ends, and a rival takes its place. Give me the rag - the red one, off the kit - and every carrot green going spare. Their schedule has company coming.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: He built the rival standing up: greens bundled loud and bright, the rag's red end flying from the knot, posted one fence post over from the rows where the raiders would have to pick a side.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Then the test: a raid dropped off the rail, caught the rag in its eye, and turned in one body. The six rows kept their leaf end to end - defended, that hour, by something that would hold still.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: He let the evening finish it: two passersby asked, and he walked them through rag, greens, and knot step by step, then sent them off with spare greens and a dare.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: Shouting only teaches the birds to wait, so he ties a decoy bundle - carrot tops, red rag, plenty of cheer - and the birds mob that instead. The patch survives, and the decoy trick spreads from base camp to base camp.

confirmBeats.speaker: narrator
confirmBeats.text: The yellow-herb bundles are heavier than they look, and Dolbur has announced he will carry the biggest one in a single trip.

departureBeats.speaker: dolbur
departureBeats.text: Yellow herbs, then! The big bundle rides my back, and the yard heard me say the word 'single' out loud. The ropes get tied at full stretch - the way my shoulders like them.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The report starts at the loading yard: the big bundle went on his back tied at a pull that made the yard's older shoulders whistle, and it held beautifully - for exactly as far as the last of the flat.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The snap came at the switchback in two voices - the belly line first, then the shoulder rope. The bundles let go down the slope, scattering yellow leaf over the grass, and nothing worth keeping was hurt except the announcement.

returnBeats.speaker: dolbur
returnBeats.text: Two ropes gone, one announcement left. Fine: the boast re-ties first, then the rope. The yard was promised delivery, not carry. The big load splits into three trips, each tied to what a rope bears.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The salvage came first: both snapped lengths picked up off the slope, the injured ends cut clean, the good parts bound into one honest working line. A broken rope, he said, is a job with a beginning and an end.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The new rule: a line earns its load by proving itself. Shorter than it started, it walked the switchback twice with nothing aboard, came back unchanged, and only then got handed something that mattered.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The split held: three loads under the rope's honest limit, walked in order with breath at the yard between trips. The two other carriers working the same switchback watched one round and split their own bundles before the afternoon ran out.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: At the gate he delivered the yard its herbs in three working loads and told the count himself: the single-carry promise failed and got named; the delivery promise held, and the thanks he earned that evening he did not argue with.

returnBeats.speaker: narrator
returnBeats.text: The ropes snap, and something in him snaps politely along with them. He repairs cheerfully and splits the load into three trips; the three-trip walk-back rhythm becomes how the trail shares heavy loads.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: The mushroom assignments are stacked on the camp table this morning, and the mushroom work is Dolbur's.

opening.speaker: dolbur
opening.text: Pio! Camp day! Belt, boots, and rations, all checked by hand this morning. Point me at the mushrooms, and I will make the assignment worth retelling.

opening.speaker: narrator
opening.text: Choose which mushroom sends Dolbur out.
